results.title: Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have reopened formal talks with ECOWAS more than a year after they quit the bloc.
results.description:
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have reopened formal talks with ECOWAS more than a year after they quit the bloc.

The first official ministerial meeting between ECOWAS and the Alliance of Sahel States took place in Dakar on 17 October. 

Both sides agreed to set up joint working groups and to push for a new cooperation arrangement built on mutual respect, good neighbourliness and sovereignty.

results.title: Fact check: Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso did leave ECOWAS.
results.description:
Fact check:

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso did leave ECOWAS. They announced withdrawal in January 2024; it took effect 29 January 2025. They formed the AES/Confederation of Sahel States.

The claim that they are now “begging to return” is false. On 17 October 2026 they held ministerial talks with ECOWAS in Dakar to negotiate a cooperation framework on trade and free movement while remaining separate. AES foreign ministers explicitly ruled out rejoining, calling speculation “no truth.”

The “Obidients hailed them / to hell with ECOWAS” part is an unverified partisan generalisation with no clear documented evidence of the movement making that collective statement.

results.title: BREAKING: MALI, NIGER AND BURKINA FASO SHAMELESSLY CRAWL BACK BEGGING AFTER 18 MONTHS OUT OF ECOWAS Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have resume
results.description:
BREAKING: MALI, NIGER AND BURKINA FASO SHAMELESSLY CRAWL BACK BEGGING AFTER 18 MONTHS OUT OF ECOWAS

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have resumed talks with ECOWAS more than 18 months after withdrawing from the regional bloc and forming the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).

The three military-led countries have now agreed with ECOWAS to establish joint working groups to develop a framework for cooperation, marking a dramatic shift after their decision to leave the organisation.

Their return to the negotiating table raises questions about the practical consequences of walking away from a regional bloc that connects West African economies through trade, movement and diplomatic cooperation. After months outside ECOWAS, the renewed talks suggest that regional realities may be harder to ignore than the political declarations that accompanied their withdrawal.

results.title: 🇷🇺Russia Tightens Its Grip on the 🌴Sahel via the Skies: An Opaque Logistics Network Between January 2025 and July 2026, pro-Russian forces c
results.description:
🇷🇺Russia Tightens Its Grip on the 🌴Sahel via the Skies: An Opaque Logistics Network

Between January 2025 and July 2026, pro-Russian forces conducted ✈️✈️ 75 flights to Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, according to ADS-B tracking data analysed by @C4ADS. 🇧🇫 Burkina Faso accounts for the bulk of the traffic, followed by Mali, while activity in Niger remains marginal. These rotations — carried out primarily by Soviet-era Antonov An-124 and Ilyushin Il-76 aircraft — sustain Africa Corps, the successor to the Wagner Group, now operating under direct Russian military command.

This aerial shuttle is more than logistical support. It forms the backbone of a grip that has consolidated since the region’s military coups. In exchange for security guarantees against groups such as JNIM and ISGS, 🇷🇺 Moscow has secured mining concessions, military bases and direct political influence, while remaining largely shielded from accountability. Civilians have paid the price through extrajudicial killings, violence and a continued deterioration of security, even as these forces have proven largely ineffective against armed groups.

Operators combine state entities — notably Flight Unit 224, the Special Flight Squadron and EMERCOM — with private companies, some already under sanctions (Aviacon Zitotrans, Rubystar, Sapsan). This hybrid model obscures attribution and preserves plausible deniability. State aircraft typically transit through Russian-controlled bases in Khmeimim (Syria) and Al-Khadim 🇱🇾(Libya), while private operators favour commercial hubs in Abu Dhabi, Algeria or Turkey. These stopovers act as potential chokepoints: disrupting access to them would significantly complicate resupply. Traffic spikes have coincided with high-level visits (including Ibrahim Traoré’s trip to Moscow in May 2025) and ground offensives. Burkina Faso functions as the main regional hub.

The transition from Wagner to Africa Corps has changed little on the ground: the same bases, routes and model of resource extraction and predation persist. The Central Sahel remains a strategic node for Russian influence in Africa, underpinned by a discreet, redundant and still difficult-to-disrupt air logistics network.
